prompt: One operator gives a busy platform an exemption from the per-minute request limit on their eVault, and that platform's servers still get 429 responses. Another operator blocks a misbehaving platform by its name, and its requests keep getting through. Why does the eVault's request limiter work this way, and what should each operator do instead?
key: Written in docs/docs/Infrastructure/eVault.md § "Rate Limiting" ("What a platform rule can and cannot do"), and implemented in GlobalRateLimiter (infrastructure/evault-core/src/core/http/global-rate-limiter.ts) with verifyPlatform in infrastructure/evault-core/src/core/auth/registry-token.ts. Every request is first held to its IP's limit (the most specific IP rule, or the IP default); only a request carrying a valid Registry token is then also held to its platform's limit. The Registry signs a token for any platform name it is asked for, so a token proves it is genuine, not who sent it: the platform name is self-declared. Two consequences follow. The IP limit is the ceiling: a platform limit or exemption never lets a caller exceed its IP limit (an exempt platform skips only the platform step), so to give a platform more headroom the operator must raise or exempt the IPs of that platform's servers as well. And a platform block is advisory: a blocked caller can request a token under another name, so to stop it the operator must block its IPs; likewise anyone can send a token carrying another platform's name and use up that platform's budget, up to their own IP limit.

sources.quote: The Registry signs a token for any platform name it is asked for, so a token proves it is genuine, not who sent it. The limiter verifies the signature and treats an invalid token as no platform at all, but the name itself is self-declared.
**The IP limit is the ceiling.** A platform limit or exemption never lets a caller exceed its IP limit. To give a platform more headroom, raise or exempt the IPs of its servers as well.

**A platform block is advisory.** A blocked caller can request a token under another name. Block its IPs to stop it. Likewise, anyone can send a token carrying another platform's name and use up that platform's budget, up to their own IP limit.

If the request carries a valid Registry token, it also counts against that platform's limit: its own rule, or the platform default. A **blocked** platform gets `403`; an **exempt** platform skips only this step.

Says the IP limit is the ceiling: a platform limit or exemption never lets a caller exceed its IP limit, so headroom needs the platform's server IPs raised or exempted
Says a platform block is advisory (a blocked caller can get a token under another name), so stopping it means blocking its IPs
